questions.question: How do plants improve soil fertility? / [CO1]
questions.solution_html:
• How do plants improve soil fertility? [U] / [CO1]
  • Plants improve soil fertility through several mechanisms
  • Adding Organic Matter: - Plant parts decompose, adding organic matter to the soil. This
  • organic matter improves soil structure, making it more porous and allowing for better water
  • infiltration and aeration.
  • Nitrogen Fixation: Legumes, like beans and peas, have a symbiotic relationship with
  • bacteria that can convert atmospheric nitrogen into a form plants can use.
  • Improving Soil Structure: Plants' roots help bind soil particles together, creating
  • aggregates that improve soil structure and enhance its ability to hold water and nutrients.
  • Nutrient Uptake and Cycling: Plants take up nutrients from the soil and then release them
  • when they decompose. This nutrient cycling helps maintain soil fertility.

questions.question: How does plant based bio manure improve soil health ? / [CO1]
questions.solution_html:
• How does plant based bio manure improve soil health ? [U] / [CO1]
  • ❖ Improves Soil Structure and Aeration: Organic manure binds soil particles together,
  • improving texture, enhancing aeration, and promoting better root penetration
  • ❖ .Increases Water-Holding Capacity: By adding organic matter, the soil can retain more
  • water, reducing the need for frequent irrigation and protecting plants against drought.
  • ❖ Boosts Microbial Activity: It serves as a food source for beneficial soil bacteria, fungi,
  • and earthworms, fostering a healthy microbiome that aids nutrient cycling.
  • ❖ Provides Slow-Release Nutrients: Unlike chemical fertilizers, it gradually releases
  • nutrients like nitrogen, phosphorus, and potassium (NPK), providing sustainable
  • nourishment to crops without toxicity.
  • ❖ Increases Soil Organic Carbon: It increases the soil organic carbon content, which acts
  • as a carbon sink and directly improves soil health indicators.
  • ❖ Suppresses Diseases and Pests: Many plant-based manures contain organic compounds
  • that have antimicrobial properties, helping to suppress soil-borne diseases.

  • Major Aspects
  • ❖ Automatic Protection: Copyright exists the moment a work is created and fixed (e.g.,

  • display, and create derivative works.

questions.question: What is layering? Name any two types of layering. / [CO3]
questions.solution_html:
• What is layering? Name any two types of layering. [K] / [CO3]
  • Layering is a plant propagation method where stems or branches are encouraged to root
  • while still attached to the parent plant. There are several types of layering, including simple,
  • compound (serpentine), mound (stool), tip, and air layering, each with a slightly different
  • approach.
  • Types of Layering:
  • Simple Layering: A stem is bent to the ground and buried in soil, encouraging root
  • development.
  • Compound (Serpentine) Layering: Multiple points along a stem are buried to create several
  • new plants from a single stem.
  • Mound (Stool) Layering: The base of a plant is cut back, and soil is piled over the new
  • shoots to promote rooting.
  • Tip Layering: Flexible stems are bent and the tips are buried in soil.
  • Air Layering: Roots are formed on a stem above ground, usually by wrapping a section of
  • the stem in a moist medium like sphagnum moss and plastic.

questions.question: Write an essay on organic farming. / [CO3] [10x1 = 10]
questions.solution_html:
• Write an essay on organic farming [U] / [CO3]
  • Organic farming is a system of agriculture that uses natural processes and resources to
  • produce food, prioritizing healthy soil, beneficial insects, and a thriving ecosystem. It
  • avoids synthetic pesticides, fertilizers, and genetically modified organisms (GMOs).
  • Instead, it relies on organic materials like crop residues, animal manures, and biological
  • pest control methods.
  • Key Practices of organic farming:
  • :
  • Soil Health: - building and maintaining healthy soil through practices like crop rotation,
  • cover cropping, composting, and minimal tillage.
  • Pest Control: Instead of synthetic pesticides, organic farmers use natural methods like
  • beneficial insects, crop rotations, and resistant varieties to control pests.
  • Fertilizers: - use organic materials like compost, animal manure, and green manure to
  • provide nutrients to crops, rather than synthetic fertilizers.
  • Water Management: - incorporates water conservation practices to ensure efficient use
  • and prevent runoff.
  • Crop Rotation: - Rotating crops helps to improve soil health, control pests and diseases,
  • and reduce the need for synthetic inputs.
  • Benefits of Organic Farming:
  • Healthier Food: - can produce food with higher nutrient content and fewer synthetic
  • residues.
  • Environmental Protection: - By avoiding synthetic chemicals, organic farming helps to
  • protect soil, water, and air quality, and promotes biodiversity.
  • Reduced Pollution: - Organic practices reduce the risk of pesticide and fertilizer
  • runoff, which can pollute waterways and harm aquatic life.
  • Improved Soil Health: - help to improve soil fertility, structure, and water-holding
  • capacity.
  • Biodiversity: - promotes biodiversity by creating habitats for beneficial insects and
  • other wildlife.
  • Challenges of Organic Farming:
  • Lower Yields:- may result in lower yields compared to conventional farming, as it
  • avoids the use of synthetic inputs that can boost crop production.
  • Higher Costs: - can be more expensive due to the cost of certified organic products and
  • the labor involved in implementing organic practices.
  • Transition Period: - Farms transitioning to organic farming may experience a period of
  • lower yields as they rebuild their soil and establish organic practices
  • (organic framing- practices adopted = 6 marks, advantages -2 marks, challenges 2

questions.question: What are the applications challenges, concerns and future prospects of Genetic Engineering? / [CO2] [10x1 = 10]
questions.solution_html:
• What are the applications challenges, concerns and future prospects of Genetic
  • Engineering?
  • Genetic engineering (GE) involves altering an organism’s DNA using technology to create
  • desired traits, with major applications in medicine (gene therapy, vaccines), agriculture (pest-
  • resistant, biofortified crops), and industry. While promising huge benefits, it faces technical
  • challenges like off-target mutations, significant environmental concerns, and ethical dilemmas
  • regarding designer babies
  • Applications of Genetic Engineering Medicine: Gene therapy to correct genetic disorders,
  • production of insulin and vaccines, and cancer treatment (e.g., CAR-T cell therapy).Agriculture:
  • Development of genetically modified (GM) crops with enhanced resistance to pests, diseases,
  • and environmental stresses (e.g., drought-resistant crops), alongside improving nutritional value.
  • Industry & Environment: Engineered microorganisms used to produce industrial enzymes,
  • biofuels, and bioremediation (cleaning up toxic waste).Research: Creating animal models to
  • understand human diseases and gene function
  • Challenges Technical Limitations: Risks of off-target effects, where unintended parts of the
  • genome are edited, leading to potential mutations .Environmental Impact: Potential for reduced
  • biodiversity, gene flow to wild species, and the creation of invasive species.
  • Economic/Regulatory: High development costs, complex regulatory approvals, and debates over
  • patenting living organisms.
  • ConcernsEthical & Social: Concerns about "designer babies" (enhancing traits rather than
  • curing diseases), genetic discrimination, and altering the human germline (inheritable
  • changes).Safety & Health: Long-term effects of consuming GM foods are still debated, although
  • scientific consensus suggests they are safe .Biosecurity: The potential to misuse technology to
  • create harmful pathogens.
  • Future ProspectsCRISPR-Cas9 Advancements: Continued refinement of gene-editing tools for
  • greater precision and efficiency. Sustainable Agriculture: Developing climate-resilient crops and
  • reducing reliance on chemical pesticides. Personalized Medicine: Tailoring treatments to an
  • individual’s genetic makeup. Synthetic Biology: Creating entirely new biological parts and
  • systems for innovative applications
  • (10×1=10)
